1.support: We, therefore, aimed to compare different PEEP-setting strategies—guided by EIT, based on lung mechanics (highest CRS), and guided by PL,EE—in patients with COVID-19-related ARDS.
1.location: p. 2, Introduction, final paragraph (also Abstract, Objectives, p. 1)

2.support: Patients that met the following criteria were included: aged ≥ 18 years; polymerase chain reaction positive for COVID-19; ARDS according to the Berlin criteria; intubated and on controlled mechanical ventilation
2.location: p. 2, Methods – Study population and setting

3.support: Data were retrospectively analyzed from a cohort study conducted between March and October 2020 in the intensive care unit of the Erasmus MC, Rotterdam, and between March and December 2021 in the intensive care unit of the Maasstad Hospital, Rotterdam.
3.location: p. 2, Methods – Study population and setting

4.support: We reviewed all clinically performed EIT-based PEEP trials during the study period (65 in total) and included 29 patients in whom simultaneous Pes and EIT recordings were performed and with adequate signal quality.

5.support: This is the largest physiological study to date comparing these methods, including multiple EIT-based approaches.

6.support: first, PEEP was stepwise increased to 10 cmH2O above baseline clinical PEEP, with a minimum of 24 cmH2O. After a stabilization period of at least 60 s, PEEP was reduced by 2 cmH2O every 30 s.

7.support: Compliance loss due to overdistension and collapse were determined as described before by Costa et al.

8.support: I looked for any statement that the persons assessing the outcomes (recommended PEEP, PL,EE, overdistension, collapse) were masked to the method applied, and found none; the report describes data acquisition and data analysis by the same authors.
8.location: Whole report; Methods (pp. 2–4) and Author contributions (p. 8)

9.support: The report describes a single-session analysis of 29 patients with no post-baseline follow-up, and all 29 included patients' data appear in every analysis (n = 29 in Table 1 and Figures 2–4); no losses after baseline are reported.

10.support: We tested the method's effect using linear mixed-effects models with the PEEP, PL,EE, collapse or overdistension as dependent variable

11.support: Outcomes were measured at each step of a single decremental PEEP titration; I found no interrupted time-series design with multiple outcome measurements before and multiple after an intervention period.
11.location: p. 2, Methods – PEEP titration; pp. 4–6, Results and Figures 2–4

12.support: PEEP titration was applied at the individual patient level (each patient underwent his/her own decremental PEEP trial); no group-level allocation or group-level intervention was used.

nih.rationale: Nine items were answered Yes: the objective is explicitly stated (item 1), eligibility criteria and the two-centre ICU cohort are clearly described (items 2 and 3), all clinically performed PEEP trials were reviewed with the 29 included patients enumerated (item 4), the titration protocol and endpoint definitions are detailed and based on the validated Costa method (items 6, 7), mixed-effects models with FDR-adjusted p values are reported (item 10) and there is no post-baseline loss of participants (item 9). The rating is lowered from Good to Fair by the absence of any statement on blinding of outcome assessors (item 8, NR), the absence of an a priori sample-size or power calculation for a 29-patient convenience sample drawn retrospectively from two cohorts with different acquisition and analysis pipelines (item 5), and the lack of an interrupted time-series with repeated pre- and post-intervention measurements (item 11, No).
